A mohel is a specially trained Jewish religious official whose specific job is to perform ritual circumcision — the surgical removal of the foreskin of the penis — on Jewish males, as required by Jewish religious law. Think of a mohel as a combination of a skilled medical practitioner and a religious authority, rolled into one person dedicated to one very specific, sacred task.
The Bigger Picture: Why Does This Role Exist?

To truly understand what a mohel is, you need to understand why the role exists.

In Judaism, circumcision is not simply a medical procedure or a cultural habit — it is one of the oldest and most sacred religious obligations in the entire faith. It is called brit milah (sometimes spelled bris milah), which means "covenant of circumcision." The word brit means "covenant," which refers to the sacred agreement between God and the Jewish people, as described in the Hebrew Bible (specifically in Genesis, where God commands Abraham to circumcise himself and all male members of his household as a sign of this covenant). Every Jewish male born since then is expected to enter into this same covenant through circumcision.

Because this act is so deeply religious and so central to Jewish identity, it cannot simply be handed off to any surgeon at a hospital. It must be performed correctly — both medically and religiously. That is precisely where the mohel comes in.
What Exactly Does a Mohel Do?

A mohel's primary responsibility is to perform the brit milah ceremony. This typically takes place on the 8th day of a male infant's life — a timing that is itself a religious requirement from the Torah. (If the baby is unwell or medically unfit, the ceremony is postponed until it is safe, but the 8th day is the standard.)

During the ceremony, the mohel:

  • Performs the circumcision with precision, skill, and the appropriate religious intent
  • Recites the required blessings in Hebrew before and during the procedure
  • Conducts or participates in the ceremony surrounding the event, which also typically involves naming the baby, offering wine, and community celebration

The mohel is therefore not just a surgeon — they are an active religious participant in a milestone ceremony. A plain surgeon in a hospital, no matter how skilled, cannot fulfill this religious role on their own.

A mohel must be trained in two distinct areas:

1. Jewish religious law (Halakha): A mohel must deeply understand the specific legal requirements of brit milah — what makes the procedure religiously valid, what the blessings are, what conditions require the ceremony to be delayed, and so on. This is not optional knowledge; it is what separates a mohel from an ordinary circumcision.

2. The surgical procedure itself: A mohel must be skilled enough to safely and precisely perform the circumcision. They learn proper technique, sterilization, care of the wound, and how to handle complications. In many modern communities, mohelim are also licensed medical doctors or nurses who have received additional religious training on top of their medical credentials. In other cases, they are religiously trained individuals who have received dedicated surgical instruction specifically in circumcision.

Mohelim are certified through recognized religious or communal institutions, and reputable mohelim take both aspects of their training seriously.

In traditional and Orthodox Jewish communities, a mohel is required to be a Jewish male who observes Jewish law. Historically, this was the universal standard.

In more liberal Jewish denominations — such as Reform, Conservative, and Reconstructionist Judaism — women can also be certified for this role. A female mohel is called a mohelet in Hebrew.

The plurals you may encounter are:

  • Mohelim — the standard Hebrew masculine plural
  • Mohelot — the Hebrew feminine plural
  • Mohels — the common anglicized plural used in everyday English
Mohel vs. Regular Doctor: What's the Difference?

This is an important distinction. A medical circumcision performed by a regular doctor in a hospital is a valid surgical procedure, but it does not fulfill the religious obligation of brit milah on its own. For the ceremony to be religiously valid according to Jewish law, it must be performed by a qualified mohel with the correct religious intention (kavanah) and the required blessings.

Some modern families have a doctor perform the medical procedure while a rabbi recites the blessings separately, but traditional religious authorities typically do not accept this arrangement as fulfilling the full obligation — they require the mohel to be the one holding the instrument.

This is why even in modern, medically advanced societies, the role of the mohel continues to exist and is actively sought out by observant Jewish families.
The Mohel's Place in the Community

A mohel is a respected and trusted figure in the Jewish community. Because brit milah is one of the first major religious events in a Jewish male's life, the mohel who performs it is often remembered and spoken of with reverence by the family for years. In smaller or tightly-knit Jewish communities, a single well-regarded mohel may perform the brit milah for multiple generations of the same family.

A mohel is a Jewish religious practitioner — trained in both religious law and surgical technique — whose dedicated role is to perform brit milah, the ritual circumcision that represents a Jewish male's entry into the ancient covenant between God and the Jewish people.
